Why can a congenital cardiac malformation first become clinically apparent in adulthood?
column2:
Congenital anatomy can acquire changing physiologic expression over time. A congenital malformation may evolve during gestation and extrauterine life; a bicuspid valve can become stenotic decades after birth.

PDF p. 15

column1: Why does a normal gross cardiac structure not exclude a congenital functional cardiac disorder?
column2:
Congenital functional abnormalities can exist without a gross structural defect. The source includes congenital complete heart block among functionally significant conditions that need not be gross structural defects.

PDF p. 15

column1: How does the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance after birth affect the interpretation of congenital circulation?
column2:
Lung expansion and falling pulmonary vascular resistance redistribute flow. Lung expansion, rising oxygen tension, reduced pulmonary resistance and elimination of the placental circulation substantially alter cardiovascular physiology.

PDF p. 15

column1: How should advanced imaging relate to the history, examination, ECG and chest radiograph?
column2:
Integrate the imaging with prior clinical observations and predicted physiology. The diagnostic approach synthesizes history, examination, ECG, radiography and advanced imaging into a coherent anatomic–physiologic explanation.

PDF p. 16

column1: Why may examination reasonably precede completion of the history in an irritable infant?
column2:
Examine while calm and integrate the history and other findings afterward. The depth and synthesis of analysis matter more than a rigid order; examining an infant during a calm interval may improve the assessment.

PDF p. 16

column1: What are the five cornerstone questions used to organize congenital cardiac recognition?
column2:
Ask about cyanosis, increased or decreased pulmonary arterial flow, the side from which the malformation originates, the dominant ventricle, and pulmonary hypertension. These organize reasoning rather than replace anatomic confirmation.

PDF p. 16

column1: Which pattern is characteristic of a Still murmur?
column2:
A Still murmur. The typical Still murmur is vibratory or buzzing, midsystolic and most prominent between the apex and lower left sternal edge in the supine child.

PDF p. 20

column1: Where are transient neonatal branch pulmonary artery systolic murmurs typically distributed?
column2:
Transient disparity between the pulmonary trunk and its branch sizes. The neonatal pulmonary trunk–branch size disparity and branch geometry can produce widely transmitted systolic turbulence; the murmur alone does not distinguish transient physiology from fixed branch stenosis.

PDF p. 21

column1: How can positional behavior support recognition of a venous hum?
column2:
A cervical venous hum. Recumbency, neutral neck position and reduced jugular flow can diminish or abolish the venous hum.

PDF p. 27

column1: What response to shoulder hyperextension supports a supraclavicular arterial systolic murmur?
column2:
Flow vibrations near the origins of the major brachiocephalic arteries. The supraclavicular arterial murmur is systolic, maximal above the clavicles and may diminish or disappear with shoulder hyperextension.

PDF p. 22

column1: Why does finding a ventricular band not establish the cause of every Still murmur?
column2:
Band prevalence persists across ages while Still murmur prevalence falls toward adolescence. The mismatch between age-related murmur prevalence and band prevalence, and the source’s explicit uncertainty, prevent treating the association as a settled universal mechanism.

PDF p. 20

column1: What qualification is needed for the statement that functional murmurs are not solely diastolic?
column2:
The source describes a rare transient neonatal ductal diastolic murmur in the first few days of life. Persistent or otherwise unexplained diastolic sounds should not be dismissed by applying an innocent-murmur label.

PDF p. 20

column1: What is meant by cardiac displacement?
column2:
Secondary cardiac displacement. Cardiac displacement is a secondary shift in intrathoracic position, such as one produced by diaphragmatic eventration.

PDF p. 30

column1: What is the purpose of sequential segmental cardiac analysis?
column2:
Identify the atria, valves, ventricles and arterial connections systematically. The source describes systematic attention to morphology, atrioventricular connections, ventriculoarterial connections and great-artery relationships.

PDF p. 31

column1: Which combined findings support mirror-image situs inversus with dextrocardia?
column2:
Situs inversus with dextrocardia. The described heart and abdominal viscera are in the mirror-image positions of the usual arrangement.

PDF p. 33

column1: Why can double discordance produce a circulation in series?
column2:
Two discordant connections restore the appropriate destinations of blood. Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance can together produce physiologic correction of blood-flow destinations.

PDF p. 31

column1: What defines right isomerism in the structures described by the source?
column2:
Right isomerism. Right isomerism describes bilateral morphologically right characteristics in structures normally different on the two sides.

PDF p. 30

column1: Why should ventricular identity not be assigned from left or right location alone?
column2:
Position can be inverted or malposed. Identify morphologic components and their atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial connections before describing the resulting circulation.

PDF p. 31

column1: How can maternal autoantibodies cause congenital complete heart block?
column2:
Transplacental transfer of maternal IgG with injury to fetal conduction tissue. The source describes passive autoimmunity involving maternal IgG antibodies, including Ro/SSA and La/SSB associations; maternal lupus can become apparent only later.

PDF p. 53

column1: Which ECG relationship establishes complete atrioventricular dissociation?
column2:
Atrial and ventricular activation are independent. In complete heart block, P waves and QRS complexes occur independently, rather than maintaining a fixed conducted relationship.

PDF p. 56

column1: Why do intermittent cannon A waves occur in complete heart block?
column2:
Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve. Independent atrial and ventricular activity can bring atrial contraction against the closed tricuspid valve, abruptly amplifying the venous A wave.

PDF p. 55

column1: Why can the first heart sound vary from beat to beat during complete heart block?
column2:
The changing atrial–ventricular timing alters valve position at ventricular systole. Because atria and ventricles beat independently, the PR relationship changes and first-sound intensity can vary widely.

PDF p. 55

column1: Can a normal-looking chest radiograph rule out congenital complete heart block?
column2:
Assess the atrial–ventricular relationship on a standard ECG. The radiographic appearance can be normal; the source emphasizes the standard ECG for establishing complete heart block.

PDF p. 59

column1: Why are narrow QRS complexes common in isolated congenital complete heart block?
column2:
The usual subsidiary pacemaker is above the bifurcation of the His bundle, preserving a normal ventricular activation sequence. The source also discusses exceptions, so QRS width is interpreted with the whole ECG.

PDF p. 59

column1: What structure may herniate through a partial left pericardial defect and alter the left cardiac border?
column2:
Herniation of the left atrial appendage through a partial left pericardial defect. Partial absence of the left pericardium may permit left atrial appendage herniation, producing the described convex left-border shadow.

PDF p. 63

column1: Which combination suggests complete congenital pericardial absence?
column2:
Loss of normal pericardial restraint. Complete absence can produce striking cardiac mobility, leftward/posterior displacement and interposed lung tissue.

PDF p. 64

column1: Which modalities establish the pericardial anatomy when echocardiography raises suspicion?
column2:
Thoracic CT or cardiac MRI. The source identifies CT and MRI as definitive modalities; echocardiography may suggest complete absence and identify coexisting defects.

PDF p. 64

column1: What is a typical chest-radiograph appearance of a congenital pericardial cyst?
column2:
A congenital pericardial cyst. A congenital pericardial cyst typically forms a smooth homogeneous density at the right cardiophrenic angle.

PDF p. 63

column1: Why can complete pericardial absence affect right-sided chamber dimensions disproportionately?
column2:
Reduced pericardial restraint particularly affects the relatively thin-walled right-sided chambers. Loss of normal pericardial constraint particularly affects the right ventricle and right atrium and can alter systemic venous return and septal motion.

PDF p. 64

column1: How does cardiac motion help distinguish partial from complete pericardial absence in this source?
column2:
Partial left absence may leave overall position and movement normal while producing focal appendage herniation. Complete absence can permit striking mobility and leftward/posterior displacement. Confirm anatomy with appropriate imaging.

PDF p. 63

column1: Which two discordances produce the physiologically corrected circulation?
column2:
Atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance. Two discordant junctions place systemic venous blood in the pulmonary circuit and pulmonary venous blood in the systemic circuit, so the circulations are in series.

PDF p. 68

column1: Which ventricular morphology supports the systemic circulation in the typical double-discordant arrangement?
column2:
The systemic morphologic right ventricle must sustain a workload for which its usual geometry and blood supply are not designed. The systemic right ventricle retains right-ventricular geometry and a morphologically right coronary supply despite systemic loading.

PDF p. 71

column1: Which morphologic valve can have an Ebstein-like malformation in the left atrioventricular position?
column2:
Morphologic tricuspid valve. The inverted left atrioventricular valve is morphologically tricuspid; Ebstein-like abnormalities and age-related regurgitation are important.

PDF p. 72

column1: What change in the long penetrating atrioventricular bundle can cause progressive block?
column2:
Replacement of conduction fibers by fibrous tissue in the long penetrating bundle. Fibrous replacement in the long penetrating bundle contributes to age-related atrioventricular block; defects may occur at several conduction levels.

PDF p. 77

column1: What precordial Q-wave pattern follows reversed septal depolarization?
column2:
Q waves in right precordial leads with absent left precordial Q waves. Inverted bundle branches activate the septum from right to left, reversing the usual precordial septal Q-wave pattern.

PDF p. 78

column1: Which echocardiographic features identify a morphologic right ventricle rather than relying on its side of the chest?
column2:
Coarse trabeculation, a moderator band, relatively distal atrioventricular valve insertion and tricuspid morphology help identify the morphologic right ventricle.

PDF p. 81

column1: What does an aortic ejection sound indicate about the level of obstruction?
column2:
A mobile stenotic aortic valve. The sound arises from abrupt movement of a mobile doming valve and identifies valvar level rather than degree.

PDF p. 96

column1: How can left ventricular failure alter an aortic stenosis murmur?
column2:
Reduced murmur intensity does not establish reduced obstruction. Aortic stenosis murmur intensity can decrease in left ventricular failure; loudness is not a stand-alone measure of obstruction.

PDF p. 97

column1: How can a bicuspid valve with a prominent false raphe be distinguished from a trileaflet valve?
column2:
Image the open valve for two unequal doming leaflets and an elliptical orifice. Open-valve imaging reveals the bicuspid anatomy that can be obscured by a false raphe during closure.

PDF p. 101

column1: What arterial pulse pattern characterizes chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
column2:
Rapid rise, wide pulse pressure and brisk collapse. Chronic severe regurgitation produces a rapid upstroke, wide pulse pressure, sometimes a bisferiens peak, and brisk collapse.

PDF p. 107

column1: Why can acute severe aortic regurgitation have a short soft diastolic murmur?
column2:
Relatively low regurgitant flow velocity can make severe acute disease acoustically unimpressive. The source describes short, medium-pitched, disarmingly soft murmurs in acute severe regurgitation; chronic peripheral signs may be absent.

PDF p. 107

column1: What does echocardiography with continuous-wave Doppler add in congenital aortic stenosis?
column2:
It defines level and morphology, estimates the transobstruction gradient and assesses ventricular dimensions and function rather than relying on murmur intensity alone.

PDF p. 101

column1: Which pulse comparison is useful for detecting coarctation?
column2:
Compare upper-extremity and femoral pulses and blood pressures. Upper–lower extremity pulse and pressure differences are hallmarks; brachial–femoral comparison is particularly practical in infants.

PDF p. 120

column1: How does the proximal aorta contribute to coarctation-associated systolic hypertension?
column2:
A stiff, poorly distensible precoarctation aorta. Increased collagen and reduced smooth muscle stiffen the proximal aorta, contributing to systolic hypertension and baroreceptor resetting.

PDF p. 116

column1: Why does absent rib notching not exclude coarctation in infancy?
column2:
Notching usually develops later through enlarged posterior intercostal collateral arteries. Collateral posterior intercostal arteries produce notching, which seldom appears before age six years.

PDF p. 126

column1: When can a neonate with severe coarctation become acutely symptomatic?
column2:
Closure of the ductus arteriosus. The source specifically associates acute neonatal symptoms in severe coarctation with ductal closure.

PDF p. 116

column1: How can femoral pulses be maintained initially in an infant with interrupted aortic arch?
column2:
Pulmonary trunk through a patent ductus into the descending aorta. Pulmonary trunk–ductus–descending aortic continuity can supply the lower body; diminishing femoral pulses can signal ductal constriction.

PDF p. 131

column1: Where may a coarctation murmur be heard in an infant when anterior auscultation is unrevealing?
column2:
Over the posterior thoracic spine near the coarctation; murmurs may diminish or disappear with heart failure.

PDF p. 124

column1: What defines a parachute mitral valve?
column2:
Parachute mitral valve. A single papillary muscle receiving all chordae defines the parachute arrangement and can restrict interchordal flow.

PDF p. 139

column1: Which obstructive lesions form the classic Shone complex?
column2:
Supravalvular mitral ring, parachute mitral valve, subaortic stenosis and coarctation. The classic four lesions are left-sided inflow/outflow obstructions; not all need be present or functionally significant.

PDF p. 139

column1: Why may congenital mitral stenosis lack a loud S1 and opening snap?
column2:
The abnormal leaflet apparatus may not make the brisk opening and closing movements required for those sounds. The characteristic brisk motion of a mobile anterior leaflet is not a feature of the congenital lesion described.

PDF p. 139

column1: Where is the typical cor-triatriatum membrane relative to the left atrial appendage?
column2:
Cor triatriatum. A membrane proximal to the appendage and valve distinguishes typical cor triatriatum from a supravalvular ring.

PDF p. 149

column1: Why can congenital pulmonary vein stenosis cause nonuniform pulmonary congestion without left atrial enlargement?
column2:
Unequal stenosis of individual pulmonary veins proximal to the left atrium. Individual veins can have different severities of narrowing, producing regional congestion while the downstream left atrium remains normal-sized.

PDF p. 149

column1: How does the partition in typical cor triatriatum divide the left atrium?
column2:
A proximal high-pressure accessory chamber receives the pulmonary veins; the distal chamber contains the left atrial appendage and fossa ovalis.

PDF p. 140

column1: What morphologic features characterize a dysplastic stenotic pulmonary valve?
column2:
Dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis. Dysplastic pulmonary stenosis has thickened separate poorly mobile leaflets without commissural fusion.

PDF p. 153

column1: How does a typical mobile pulmonary-valve ejection sound change with inspiration?
column2:
Reduced additional cephalad movement of a mobile pulmonary valve during ventricular contraction. Inspiration prepositions the mobile valve cephalad through increased right atrial contraction, reducing further excursion and the ejection sound.

PDF p. 161

column1: Can pinpoint neonatal pulmonary stenosis produce a soft murmur?
column2:
Pinpoint pulmonary stenosis can have a deceptively soft murmur. The source emphasizes that pinpoint neonatal stenosis may sound disarmingly soft despite severe obstruction.

PDF p. 161

column1: Why can the pulmonary component of S2 remain normal in branch pulmonary artery stenosis?
column2:
The central pulmonary diastolic pressure can remain normal or nearly normal at valve closure. Branch stenosis can raise central systolic pressure while pressure falls to near-normal diastolic levels, so valve closure need not be accentuated.

PDF p. 164

column1: What diastolic murmur pattern is described in isolated low-pressure congenital pulmonary regurgitation?
column2:
Short delayed low-to-medium-frequency crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the upper left sternal border. The source describes a distinctive short delayed low-to-medium-frequency diastolic murmur, sometimes louder with inspiration.

PDF p. 175

column1: How does a double-chambered right ventricle create obstruction?
column2:
Obstructing intracavitary muscle bundles divide the right ventricle into a high-pressure inlet portion and a lower-pressure outlet portion; a ventricular septal defect commonly coexists.

PDF p. 153

column1: What is the atrialized right ventricle in Ebstein anatomy?
column2:
The inlet right ventricle between the anatomic annulus and displaced functional valve. Apical displacement atrializes the proximal inlet right ventricle while the trabecular and outlet portions form the functional right ventricle.

PDF p. 180

column1: Why may prominent systolic jugular V waves be absent despite severe Ebstein-related regurgitation?
column2:
A large compliant right atrium and toneless atrialized ventricle damp low-pressure regurgitant flow. Commodious right-sided chambers and low-pressure hypokinetic regurgitation can damp the expected jugular signs.

PDF p. 183

column1: How can neonatal cyanosis improve and recur years later in Ebstein anomaly?
column2:
A neonatal right-to-left atrial shunt can diminish as pulmonary resistance falls and reappear when abnormal right ventricular filling pressure rises. The source describes this uncommon course through changing right-sided filling conditions and interatrial shunting.

PDF p. 182

column1: Which ECG finding supports preexcitation rather than short PR alone?
column2:
Preexcitation. Early delta-wave inscription supports preexcitation; a short PR interval alone can occasionally occur without a delta wave or tachycardia history.

PDF p. 187

column1: What should echocardiography assess beyond displaced tricuspid leaflet anatomy?
column2:
Identify a PFO or secundum defect and determine interatrial shunt direction. Color flow imaging and Doppler identify the atrial pathway and whether right-to-left shunting coexists.

PDF p. 190

column1: What distinctive electrical-mechanical combination characterizes the atrialized right ventricle?
column2:
It generates a ventricular intracavitary electrogram but an atrial-type pressure pulse, unlike the functional right ventricle.

PDF p. 182

column1: What mainly determines shunt volume across a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect?
column2:
Relative compliance of the two ventricles. With little atrial pressure difference, preferential filling of the more compliant right ventricle produces the usual left-to-right shunt.

PDF p. 204

column1: Where does the typical midsystolic murmur of a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect originate?
column2:
Increased flow through the pulmonary outflow and pulmonary trunk. The systolic murmur reflects augmented pulmonary flow, not a high-velocity jet across the nonrestrictive atrial communication.

PDF p. 210

column1: What does fixed splitting mean?
column2:
Wide fixed splitting. Fixed denotes unchanged separation with respiration; persistent splitting remains audible but varies in width.

PDF p. 211

column1: What imaging-clinical combination supports obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection?
column2:
Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous connection. Obstructed anomalous venous return can produce severe neonatal hypoxemia and congestion with an unimpressive heart size and attenuated flow murmur.

PDF p. 237

column1: What leaflet arrangement permits both atrial and ventricular shunting in a complete common atrioventricular canal?
column2:
Communication at both atrial and ventricular levels. Free-floating bridging leaflets permit both atrial and ventricular components of the complete canal.

PDF p. 239

column1: How does persistent PFO differ from a true secundum tissue defect?
column2:
A PFO retains a valve at the fossa ovalis that has not fused completely; a true secundum defect represents deficient septal tissue rather than simply persistence of the flap-valve channel.

PDF p. 197

column1: What typical combination accompanies severe pulmonary valve stenosis and a right-to-left atrial shunt?
column2:
Patent foramen ovale. Severe pulmonary stenosis with right-to-left shunting most often uses a patent foramen ovale; a nonrestrictive secundum defect more often accompanies mild-to-moderate stenosis and left-to-right flow.

PDF p. 254

column1: How can severe pulmonary stenosis generate a presystolic right-to-left atrial shunt?
column2:
High right atrial pressure stretches the foramen and drives blood toward the left atrium. Forceful atrial contraction raises right atrial pressure, increases PFO patency and can generate a presystolic right-to-left shunt.

PDF p. 254

column1: How does warmth help distinguish peripheral low-flow cyanosis from a central shunt contribution?
column2:
A low-skin-flow peripheral component has improved; central shunt cyanosis must still be assessed. Warmth improves skin blood flow and can diminish peripheral cyanosis while making any persistent central component easier to recognize.

PDF p. 254

column1: What auscultatory additions suggest pulmonary valve stenosis in a nonrestrictive atrial septal defect?
column2:
Coexisting mobile pulmonary valve stenosis. The combination adds valvar ejection sound, a longer louder stenotic murmur and further delay and softening of P2 to the atrial-shunt findings.

PDF p. 257

column1: Which imaging tools establish the valve obstruction and atrial shunt direction?
column2:
Doppler for the obstructive gradient and color flow for the interatrial shunt. Imaging identifies the valve and interatrial pathway; Doppler assesses the gradient and color flow confirms shunt direction.

PDF p. 261

column1: Why does raised right atrial pressure with an atrial communication increase paradoxical embolic risk?
column2:
It can promote right-to-left passage across a PFO or atrial defect, allowing systemic venous embolic material access to the arterial circulation.

PDF p. 254

column1: What makes a ventricular septal defect restrictive?
column2:
Restrictive defect. Restriction at the defect limits pressure transmission and shunt flow, leaving a systolic pressure difference.

PDF p. 267

column1: Why can a sizable ventricular left-to-right shunt become symptomatic after the newborn period?
column2:
Falling pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right flow. The neonatal fall in pulmonary resistance permits a larger shunt and pulmonary venous return, imposing left ventricular volume load.

PDF p. 270

column1: How can pulmonary vascular disease reverse a nonrestrictive ventricular shunt?
column2:
Right-to-left shunting from pulmonary vascular disease. With equal ventricular systolic pressures, relative vascular resistances govern flow; suprasystemic pulmonary resistance favors reversal.

PDF p. 268

column1: Why may the murmur shorten and soften as pulmonary vascular resistance rises?
column2:
Reduced left-to-right flow can reflect worsening pulmonary vascular disease. As pulmonary resistance approaches systemic, the left-to-right murmur can shorten, soften and eventually disappear with reversal.

PDF p. 275

column1: Which valve abnormality should be sought when a ventricular defect is accompanied by aortic regurgitation?
column2:
Aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation. Perimembranous and subarterial defects can be associated with aortic cusp prolapse; regurgitant volume can explain disproportionate left ventricular enlargement.

PDF p. 288

column1: How can perimembranous ventricular defects close spontaneously?
column2:
Adherence of septal tricuspid leaflet tissue to the defect margins is a common mechanism and can be associated with a membranous septal aneurysm.

PDF p. 266

column1: Which malalignment links the principal anatomy of tetralogy of Fallot?
column2:
Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum. Outlet septal malalignment creates the ventricular defect, narrows right ventricular outflow and contributes to aortic override.

PDF p. 297

column1: What chiefly determines shunt direction in classic tetralogy with a nonrestrictive defect?
column2:
More right-to-left flow into the aorta and less pulmonary flow. Relative outflow and systemic resistances determine the balance; severe outflow obstruction diverts blood toward the aorta.

PDF p. 301

column1: Why can the pulmonary stenotic murmur soften during a hypoxic spell?
column2:
A sharp decline in forward pulmonary blood flow. Less blood traverses the stenotic pulmonary outflow, so the murmur shortens and softens despite worsening hypoxemia.

PDF p. 309

column1: How can squatting improve oxygenation in an unrepaired tetralogy circulation?
column2:
Increased systemic resistance and reduced return of desaturated leg blood. Squatting can redirect right ventricular flow toward the lungs and curtail desaturated lower-extremity venous return.

PDF p. 307

column1: Why is right ventricular systolic pressure usually systemic in classic tetralogy?
column2:
The ventricle can decompress through the communication into the systemic outlet. The nonrestrictive defect imposes a systemic pressure ceiling; partial occlusion or true restriction can remove that protection.

PDF p. 302

column1: Why can pulmonary atresia in this anatomy coexist with only mild cyanosis?
column2:
Abundant systemic-to-pulmonary collateral flow can supply effective pulmonary gas exchange despite absent forward right ventricular pulmonary flow.

PDF p. 301

column1: How does this source pragmatically define double outlet right ventricle?
column2:
Double outlet right ventricle. The chapter uses ventricular support of most of both arterial valves as its pragmatic definition while acknowledging classification debates.

PDF p. 326

column1: Where does left ventricular blood preferentially stream with a subpulmonary ventricular communication?
column2:
Left ventricular blood preferentially enters the pulmonary trunk. A subpulmonary communication directs left ventricular output toward the pulmonary outlet, creating a transposition-like physiology.

PDF p. 331

column1: What physiology can subaortic double outlet right ventricle without pulmonary stenosis resemble?
column2:
A large ventricular left-to-right shunt with increased pulmonary flow. Low pulmonary resistance permits increased pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, resembling a large isolated ventricular defect.

PDF p. 327

column1: How does pulmonary stenosis change subaortic double outlet physiology?
column2:
Less pulmonary flow and more blood directed to the aorta. Obstruction diverts both ventricular streams away from the pulmonary outlet and toward the aorta, producing a tetralogy-like pattern.

PDF p. 327

column1: Why can a restrictive ventricular communication be hazardous in double outlet right ventricle?
column2:
Obstruction to left ventricular egress and subaortic flow. The communication is an essential left ventricular exit; restriction can act as subaortic stenosis rather than a uniformly favorable reduction in shunt.

PDF p. 326

column1: What does atrioventricular valve straddling mean?
column2:
Chordal attachments insert on both sides of the ventricular septum; this differs from overriding, which describes biventricular commitment of the valve annulus.

PDF p. 327

column1: Where are the usual aortic and pulmonary openings of a patent ductus?
column2:
Patent ductus arteriosus. The normal ductal insertion is near the left pulmonary artery, with its aortic end distal to the left subclavian artery.

PDF p. 346

column1: How does a left-to-right ductal shunt load the left ventricle?
column2:
Increased pulmonary venous return imposes left ventricular volume load. Pulmonary recirculation returns to the left atrium and ventricle, increasing left-heart volume load.

PDF p. 351

column1: How does the classic uncomplicated ductal murmur relate to the second sound?
column2:
Classic continuous ductal murmur. The classic ductal sound envelops the second heart sound with continuous systolic-to-diastolic flow.

PDF p. 358

column1: Why can a reversed ductal shunt cause cyanotic toes with a pink right hand?
column2:
Pulmonary arterial blood entering the descending aorta through a ductus distal to the right-arm supply. The ductal entry usually delivers desaturated blood to the lower body after the proximal arch vessels have branched.

PDF p. 355

column1: Why does reversed flow through an aortopulmonary window usually lack differential cyanosis?
column2:
Desaturated blood enters proximal to systemic arch distribution. A window delivers blood into the ascending aorta, unlike the usual distal ductal insertion.

PDF p. 367

column1: Why can a clinically silent ductus remain patent?
column2:
Jet direction and pressure-flow conditions can prevent an audible murmur; Doppler imaging can identify patency despite absent auscultatory signs.

PDF p. 351

column1: Why can ischemia emerge after the neonatal fall in pulmonary pressure?
column2:
Falling pulmonary pressure reduces antegrade perfusion through the anomalous artery. Initially high pulmonary pressure can support antegrade flow. Its postnatal fall reduces that supply unless intercoronary perfusion becomes adequate.

PDF p. 373

column1: How can intercoronary collateral flow both help and harm in pulmonary-origin left coronary anatomy?
column2:
Collaterals restore some perfusion but also permit a low-resistance coronary steal. The collateral route can nourish myocardium while also bypassing capillaries toward a low-pressure pulmonary outlet.

PDF p. 374

column1: Why can anomalous left coronary origin cause mitral regurgitation?
column2:
Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction. Papillary muscle ischemia can impair mitral competence and add regurgitant volume to an already compromised ventricle.

PDF p. 377

column1: Which ECG pattern should raise suspicion for pulmonary-origin left coronary artery in a symptomatic infant?
column2:
Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary trunk. Deep narrow lateral q waves, often with left ventricular hypertrophy and a leftward axis, are a characteristic clue; early infant tracings can be less conspicuous.

PDF p. 379

column1: What imaging observation separates anomalous coronary origin from a coronary-to-pulmonary fistula?
column2:
Define whether the left coronary arises from the pulmonary trunk or from its normal aortic sinus. An anomalous left coronary lacks its normal aortic origin; a coronary arterial fistula can have similar pulmonary flow while both coronary arteries retain aortic origins.

PDF p. 381

column1: Does asymptomatic survival to adulthood establish that a pulmonary-origin left coronary artery is benign?
column2:
No. Adult presentations can include mitral regurgitation, ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest or sudden death despite little earlier symptom burden.

PDF p. 376

column1: What defines a typical congenital coronary arterial fistula?
column2:
Congenital coronary arterial fistula. A fistulous branch provides an abnormal drainage route despite usually appropriate coronary origins.

PDF p. 385

column1: Why can a large coronary-to-right atrial fistula load both ventricles?
column2:
Left-to-right recirculation with right and left ventricular volume loading. Blood enters the right atrium and traverses the right heart, lungs and left heart before returning to the aorta.

PDF p. 386

column1: How can a coronary fistula cause ischemia without a very large pulmonary shunt?
column2:
Low-resistance runoff can divert coronary blood away from myocardium. Myocardial steal depends on the low-resistance alternative pathway and the coronary territory involved, not only total pulmonary shunt size.

PDF p. 386

column1: What chiefly determines where a coronary fistula murmur is loudest?
column2:
The chamber or vessel receiving the fistula. The drainage site determines the intracardiac sound source and corresponding thoracic location.

PDF p. 389

column1: What murmur can a coronary-to-left ventricular fistula generate?
column2:
Aortic-to-ventricular pressure difference favors diastolic fistulous flow. A coronary-to-left ventricular communication can produce an early diastolic murmur; systolic flow depends on the stoma and compression pattern.

PDF p. 390

column1: How does the feeding coronary artery often appear proximal to a fistula?
column2:
It is often dilated, elongated and tortuous, while distal coronary branches may remain of normal caliber.

PDF p. 385

column1: Where does a noncoronary sinus aneurysm most often rupture?
column2:
Right atrium. The noncoronary sinus is anatomically related to the right atrium; right coronary sinus aneurysms commonly enter the right ventricle or sometimes the right atrium.

PDF p. 396

column1: Why can a sudden large sinus rupture cause rapid congestive failure?
column2:
The heart has little time to adapt to the acute shunt volume burden. Size, rapidity and receiving chamber determine the burden; sudden substantial recirculation can overwhelm adaptation.

PDF p. 396

column1: What should a new continuous murmur with acute symptoms suggest in someone with a ventricular septal defect?
column2:
Rupture of a coexisting sinus of Valsalva aneurysm. The source highlights this change as a clue to an aortic sinus aneurysm rupturing into the right side of the heart.

PDF p. 399

column1: How may a sinus rupture murmur differ from a classic ductal murmur?
column2:
A ruptured aortic sinus communication is plausible. Sinus rupture murmurs can be continuous without the characteristic second-sound peak of the classic ductal murmur.

PDF p. 402

column1: How can an aortic sinus aneurysm cause atrioventricular block?
column2:
Injury to the AV node or His bundle near the septal base. Ruptured or unruptured aneurysms penetrating the septal base can disrupt nearby conduction tissue.

PDF p. 403

column1: Can an unruptured sinus aneurysm produce a to-and-fro murmur?
column2:
Yes. Flow into and out of the intact pouch can cause murmurs in both phases; color Doppler assessment is needed to distinguish this from an actual perforation.

PDF p. 403

column1: How does systemic venous blood reach the left heart in pulmonary atresia with an intact ventricular septum?
column2:
Right-to-left flow through an interatrial communication. The interatrial communication is the right atrium’s exit to the left heart; its restriction can add to the circulatory problem.

PDF p. 410

column1: Why is ductal patency crucial in the usual unrepaired neonatal circulation?
column2:
Effective pulmonary blood flow can cease. The ductus supplies the pulmonary circuit in the usual anatomy; systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals are generally inadequate.

PDF p. 410

column1: Does pulmonary atresia with an intact septum always imply a tiny right ventricle?
column2:
Both patterns occur, and tricuspid competence helps explain their different appearances. The chapter describes a common small-ventricle pattern and a less common dilated pattern associated with an incompetent dysplastic or Ebstein-like valve.

PDF p. 407

column1: What makes some coronary circulations right ventricular dependent?
column2:
High right ventricular systolic pressure drives retrograde coronary flow. When aortic access is obstructed, myocardial perfusion can depend on suprasystemic right ventricular pressure supplying the coronary bed.

PDF p. 410

column1: Can a small thick-walled right ventricle lack prominent ECG evidence of RV hypertrophy?
column2:
The small cavity can generate little right ventricular electrical amplitude despite its thick wall. The source describes absent prominent RV hypertrophy voltage in the small-ventricle pattern; chamber geometry and cavity size matter.

PDF p. 414

column1: What does functional pulmonary atresia mean in the source’s distinction?
column2:
A dilated mechanically inadequate right ventricle cannot generate enough pressure to open a stenotic but anatomically nonatretic pulmonary valve, often with severe tricuspid regurgitation.

PDF p. 407

column1: How does systemic venous blood reach the ventricle in tricuspid atresia?
column2:
Right-to-left flow across an interatrial communication. Systemic venous blood must cross from right atrium to left atrium and pass through the patent left AV valve.

PDF p. 418

column1: Why can spontaneous VSD closure be harmful in tricuspid atresia with normally related great arteries?
column2:
Increasing subpulmonary obstruction limits lung flow. With normally related arteries, the ventricular communication provides access to the pulmonary circuit; narrowing can produce acquired pulmonary atresia.

PDF p. 418

column1: What can a restrictive VSD obstruct when tricuspid atresia is accompanied by transposed great arteries?
column2:
Subaortic obstruction to systemic output. In this arrangement left ventricular blood must traverse the defect to reach the transposed aorta; restriction creates subaortic stenosis.

PDF p. 418

column1: What ECG pattern supports the common non-transposed form with a restrictive ventricular defect?
column2:
Left-axis deviation with adult-like precordial progression and right atrial P waves. The source summary describes left-axis deviation, counterclockwise depolarization, adult precordial progression and right atrial P waves in this common arrangement.

PDF p. 430

column1: What does echocardiography with color flow and Doppler establish in tricuspid atresia?
column2:
Echocardiography with color flow and Doppler. Echo identifies the echodense absent connection, chamber sizes, great arterial relationships and shunt or obstruction physiology.

PDF p. 429

column1: Why can mild cyanosis coexist with heart failure in tricuspid atresia?
column2:
A nonrestrictive ventricular defect and low pulmonary vascular resistance can cause excessive pulmonary flow and left ventricular volume overload, reducing cyanosis at the price of heart failure.

PDF p. 420

column1: What anatomic connection defines a morphologic univentricular heart?
column2:
A morphologically defined single ventricular connection. The chapter defines the anatomy by atrial and AV connections to one main ventricular chamber, distinguishing it from other functionally single-ventricle categories.

PDF p. 433

column1: How does pulmonary flow influence presentation in a single-ventricle heart?
column2:
Excess pulmonary flow with ventricular volume overload. Excess pulmonary flow produces heart failure and poor growth despite relatively mild cyanosis.

PDF p. 440

column1: Can systemic and pulmonary venous streams remain partly separate within a single ventricle?
column2:
Preferential streaming can direct oxygenated blood toward the aorta. The source describes partial stream separation influenced by outlet arrangement and pulmonary resistance.

PDF p. 440

column1: Why can progressive restriction of the outlet foramen worsen single-left-ventricle physiology?
column2:
Subaortic obstruction with diversion toward the pulmonary circuit and greater volume burden. Restriction creates subaortic stenosis and may augment already excessive pulmonary flow and ventricular volume overload.

PDF p. 441

column1: Why can a pulmonary stenotic murmur shorten and soften as obstruction worsens in a single-ventricle heart?
column2:
Less blood crosses the increasingly obstructed pulmonary outlet. As stenosis increases, more flow is diverted to the systemic outlet and less traverses the pulmonary obstruction, reducing its murmur.

PDF p. 441

column1: What associated structure should be assessed when subaortic stenosis has existed from infancy in a single-left-ventricle heart?
column2:
The aortic arch should be assessed for coarctation or hypoplasia using appropriate imaging and Doppler, because these may accompany a restrictive systemic outlet.

PDF p. 448

column1: Which atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial connections define complete transposition?
column2:
AV concordance with ventriculoarterial discordance and parallel circuits. Complete transposition combines AV concordance and ventriculoarterial discordance, creating parallel systemic and pulmonary recirculation.

PDF p. 451

column1: Why can increasing pulmonary flow fail to correct systemic hypoxemia when the atrial communication is restrictive?
column2:
Oxygenated blood recirculates through the pulmonary circuit instead of adequately entering systemic flow. An adequate communication permits exchange between the circuits; a restrictive atrial route can leave oxygenated blood trapped in pulmonary recirculation.

PDF p. 457

column1: Can an early neonatal ECG be normal in complete transposition?
column2:
A normal early ECG does not exclude the abnormal arterial connections. The chapter explicitly describes a potentially normal ECG in the first days; structural assessment remains essential.

PDF p. 461

column1: What can cause reversed differential cyanosis in complete transposition with a large ductus and pulmonary vascular disease?
column2:
More oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood enters the descending aorta beyond the left subclavian artery. Oxygenated pulmonary arterial blood can pass through the ductus to the lower body, producing less cyanotic feet.

PDF p. 458

column1: What produces the characteristic egg-like cardiac silhouette in complete transposition with increased pulmonary flow?
column2:
A prominent right atrium and convex enlarged left ventricle shape the silhouette. The right atrium forms the blunter right border and the enlarged left ventricle the convex left border; arterial arrangement contributes to the narrow pedicle.

PDF p. 464

column1: Why is coronary anatomy important even if it does not determine the initial physiology of complete transposition?
column2:
The origins and proximal courses are anatomically pivotal for an arterial switch operation; they must be defined rather than assumed from the usual pattern.

PDF p. 451

column1: Which arterial beds arise from the common trunk?
column2:
Truncus arteriosus. A single great artery and single semilunar valve supply the three circulations.

PDF p. 472

column1: How does type 1 truncus differ from a pattern with separate pulmonary branch ostia?
column2:
Type 1 truncus. Type 1 has a short main pulmonary artery from the trunk; separate branch ostia constitute the other grouped pattern.

PDF p. 472

column1: Why can cyanosis diminish while heart failure worsens in an infant with truncus arteriosus?
column2:
Falling pulmonary resistance increases lung flow and ventricular volume load. More pulmonary flow improves systemic oxygenation but imposes volume overload and may cause severe heart failure.

PDF p. 475

column1: Why can truncal valve regurgitation produce biventricular failure?
column2:
Regurgitant flow is received by both ventricles and adds to their burden. The biventricular truncus permits regurgitant volume to load both ventricles, adding to existing hemodynamic stress.

PDF p. 475

column1: What associated syndrome should be considered with truncus, hypocalcemia and deficient cellular immunity?
column2:
DiGeorge syndrome. The chapter describes DiGeorge-related thymic and parathyroid deficiency with truncus arteriosus.

PDF p. 479

column1: What imaging observations define truncal valve dysfunction?
column2:
Color flow imaging assesses regurgitation, and continuous-wave Doppler assesses stenosis, alongside valve morphology and the pulmonary branching anatomy.

PDF p. 482

column1: What is the usual isolated physiologic effect of a left SVC draining through the coronary sinus to the right atrium?
column2:
The route is usually physiologically harmless despite coronary sinus dilation. Blood still reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus, so an isolated connection need not create a physiologic derangement.

PDF p. 486

column1: How can a left SVC-to-left atrial connection coexist with absent cyanosis?
column2:
Left atrium to left SVC, across the bridge and into the right SVC. A freely communicating bridge can permit left-to-right flow from left atrium through the venous pathway to right atrium, reversing the expected cyanotic pattern.

PDF p. 486

column1: What route is described in isolated IVC interruption with azygos continuation?
column2:
Azygos continuation, which can be physiologically insignificant in isolation. The interrupted inferior caval flow continues through a dilated azygos system to the right SVC; isolated cases need not cause a shunt.

PDF p. 486

column1: What congenital venous connection should be considered with an unexpectedly dilated coronary sinus?
column2:
Persistent left superior vena cava. An unexpectedly enlarged coronary sinus can be the clue to an unsuspected left SVC; color and contrast studies define the route.

PDF p. 490

column1: Why may a cyanotic patient with anomalous caval-to-left atrial drainage lack right ventricular hypertrophy?
column2:
Right-heart flow is normal or reduced because some systemic venous blood bypasses it. Anomalous caval return bypasses the right heart, unlike lesions with major RV pressure or volume overload.

PDF p. 490

column1: What neurologic complications can occur despite few symptoms in isolated caval drainage to the left atrium?
column2:
Paradoxical embolism and brain abscess have been reported; modest hemodynamic burden does not eliminate complications of bypassing the pulmonary circulation.

PDF p. 489

column1: Why can a pulmonary arteriovenous fistula cause cyanosis without major ventricular volume overload?
column2:
Blood bypasses gas exchange while flow through uninvolved lung may fall reciprocally. The right-to-left intrapulmonary route bypasses the capillary bed; redistribution can limit the net increase in ventricular flow.

PDF p. 493

column1: What inherited disorder links recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectases and pulmonary AV malformations?
column2:
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. The source describes an autosomal dominant vasculopathy with mucocutaneous bleeding and visceral arteriovenous malformations.

PDF p. 493

column1: Why should auscultation extend beyond the precordium when a pulmonary AV fistula is suspected?
column2:
A peripheral pulmonary fistula can generate a localized flow murmur. Peripheral fistulae transmit sounds to the overlying chest wall; inspiratory flow and reduced compression may increase audibility.

PDF p. 499

column1: What does delayed left atrial contrast after a venous bubble injection usually suggest in this source?
column2:
A pulmonary right-to-left shunt. The chapter describes delayed appearance beyond three cycles as usually indicating pulmonary shunting; the timing is a clue interpreted with anatomy.

PDF p. 500

column1: What important neurologic risks accompany pulmonary AV fistulae?
column2:
Paradoxical embolism, stroke and brain abscess. The shunt bypasses the pulmonary filter; the source highlights embolic events and brain abscess.

PDF p. 498

column1: What radiographic finding helps identify a pulmonary fistula rather than a nonspecific lung nodule?
column2:
A round or lobulated intrapulmonary density may have vascular shadows linking it to the hilum, representing afferent and efferent channels; small diffuse lesions may be poorly defined.

PDF p. 500

column1: How is the systemic circulation supplied in the aortic-atresia form of hypoplastic left heart?
column2:
Right ventricle through pulmonary trunk, ductus and descending aorta. The pulmonary artery/ductus/descending aortic continuity provides systemic flow; retrograde flow supplies the small ascending aorta and coronary origins.

PDF p. 503

column1: Why is ductal constriction dangerous in aortic-atresia hypoplastic left heart?
column2:
Reduced systemic and retrograde coronary perfusion impairs output and RV function. The ductus supports systemic and coronary supply; constriction compromises both and can worsen the sole pumping ventricle.

PDF p. 503

column1: Why can falling pulmonary resistance produce a shock-like state despite relatively high oxygen saturation?
column2:
Flow is preferentially diverted to the lungs at the expense of systemic output. The right ventricle supplies both beds; increasing lung flow can improve mixing saturation while reducing systemic blood flow.

PDF p. 505

column1: Can hypoplastic left heart present with little or no murmur?
column2:
A severe ductal-dependent left-heart lesion remains possible. The source emphasizes unimpressive auscultation despite dramatic illness; aortic atresia leaves a single pulmonary closure sound.

PDF p. 506

column1: Why does restrictive left atrial egress matter in hypoplastic left heart?
column2:
Pulmonary venous return encounters an obstructed left atrium. The left atrium needs an alternative exit when mitral inflow is severely limited; atrial restriction compromises that exit and promotes congestion.

PDF p. 503

column1: Which echocardiographic findings should be assessed beyond left ventricular size?
column2:
Define the aortic and mitral valves, atrial septum, ductal and arch pathways, retrograde ascending aortic flow, RV function and tricuspid competence.

PDF p. 508

column1: Why does an ectopic coronary origin require definition of the proximal course?
column2:
Whether its course is anterior, retroaortic, interarterial or intramyocardial. The source emphasizes that the route relative to the great arteries can be more important than the ectopic origin itself.

PDF p. 517

column1: Which anomalous coronary arrangement carries the greatest risk in the chapter’s comparison?
column2:
Left main from the right sinus passing between aorta and RV outflow tract. The source identifies the left main or major left branch passing between the aorta and RV outflow tract as particularly concerning; ostial shape and exercise also affect risk.

PDF p. 518

column1: How does absence of a left main trunk differ from left main ostial atresia?
column2:
Absence of a common left main trunk, generally functionally benign. Separate patent LAD and circumflex origins are different from a blind or imperforate left main origin.

PDF p. 515

column1: Why is a coronary artery crossing the RV outflow tract important in tetralogy of Fallot?
column2:
It may create major surgical risk despite little baseline physiologic effect. A coronary crossing the outflow tract can be endangered during intervention even when its resting physiologic effect is small.

PDF p. 519

column1: What permits survival when the left main coronary ostium is congenitally atretic?
column2:
Adequate channels from a normally arising right coronary artery. Survival depends on adequate connections from the right coronary artery to the distal left system; presentation can span infancy to adulthood.

PDF p. 518

column1: Why is a single coronary artery not automatically equivalent to clinically dangerous coronary flow?
column2:
A single ostium can give rise to normally formed and distributed branches; significance depends on factors including major branch hypoplasia and a potentially hazardous proximal course.
